system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2148-09-16 20:49:00 to 2148-09-23 16:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic systolic heart failure, and atrial fibrillation was admitted with chest pain, shortness of breath, and tachycardia after missing a dialysis session and medications due to severe nausea and vomiting. He had used crack cocaine recently, which contributed to atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. On admission, he was volume overloaded with mild pulmonary edema and a right pleural effusion. He underwent three hemodialysis sessions, removing over 4 liters of fluid, which resolved his symptoms. His heart rate was controlled with diltiazem and metoprolol, and he was discharged on his home regimen with the addition of daily aspirin for stroke prevention. Suicidal ideation expressed in the ED was retracted, with the patient stating he was overwhelmed by illness. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned with nephrology and primary care.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure

Brief Hospital Course:
___ M PMHx DM, HTN, ESRD on HD ___, CHF (EF 28%), afib,

# Hypoxia: He presented with hypoxia in the setting of missed 
dialysis session and active crack cocaine smoking. His CXR 
showed pulmonary edema but PNA could not be ruled out so he was 
treated for possible co-existing health-care associated 
pneumonia with broad spectrum antibiotics. Echo showed stable to 
mildy depressed EF though unlikley to be cause of his pulmonary 
edema. He underwent multiple sessions of dialysis and his 
respiratory status significantly improved. His antibiotics were 
stopped and he was transferred to the floor where he remained 
afebrile and was weaned off room air. He was satting 95% on RA 
at the time of discharge and denied SOB.
  
# Left-sided Chest Pain: The patient has been admitted multiple 
times for chest pain thought to be musckuloskeletal chest pain. 
He again had chest pain here without associated EKG 
abonormalities that was not relieved with nitroglycerin. He did 
have elevated troponins though he has elevated troponins at 
baseline. The pain was easily reproducible on palpation and 
improved with removal of his tunneled dialysis catheter. He was 
treated with percocet with good response. On the floor, he had 
recurrence of chest pain. On review of records, it was noted 
that his chest pain tended to occur in conjunction with RVR 
during previous admissions. This was found to be the case here 
as well, as CP occurred when rate began to run over 120-130s. 
RVR was managed as below and symptomatic relief for CP was 
otherwise provided with small doses of IV dilaudid to good 
effect (0.25mg IV q6h prn). Pt denied CP at the time of 
discharge and rate was well-controlled as below.
  
# Atrial fibrillation/Flutter: He is chronically in 
afib/flutter. He has been well rate controlled here on Diltiazem 
and digoxin. Of note he is not on metoprolol because of his 
active cocaine use. During his admission his digoxin level was 
high on his home dose so his schedule was changed so that he 
would received Digoxin after HD with trough levels drawn 
pre-dialysis. He is on full dose aspirin but not warfarin 
because of history of GI bleeding. He had two episodes of RVR on 
the floor with rates into the 160-170s. This was managed with 
diltiazem IV push 10mg on both occasions and his daily diltiazem 
dose was increased to 420mg from 360mg daily. It was noted that 
holding his diltiazem until after HD led to RVR so plan was made 
to take diltiazem every day at 12pm instead of in the morning. 
rate well-controlled in 80-90s on this dose.
  
# ESRD: He receives HD ___ as an oupatient. He has had 
multiple admission in the setting of missed dialysis. He 
underwent multiple dialysis sessions with improvement in his 
symptoms as above. He was transitioned back to his three times 
weekly schedule. His tunneled dialysis catheter was removed 
because he has a functional fistula. We continued nephrocaps, 
cinacalcet, sevelamer carbonate.
  
# DMII. Lantus and sliding scale insulin were continued. He did 
have mild hypoglycemia so his sliding scale was adjusted.
  
# Diabetic Neuropathy: Continued gabapentin 100mg TID

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been having trouble breathing all day. Started yesterday after I had bad diarrhea. I missed my dialysis because of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any chest pain or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, left side chest pain, sharp but only lasts a few seconds. And I felt chills, like I had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see in your chart you used crack cocaine this morning. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, just once. I know it’s bad, but I’ve been stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important we’re honest so we can help you. That likely contributed to your fast heart rate. We’re going to start you on oxygen and run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows fluid in your lungs—moderate to severe pulmonary edema. That’s why you’re short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from missing dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Your body holds onto fluid when you miss dialysis, and it can back up into your lungs. We’ll get you on dialysis as soon as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My potassium is high again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 8.3, which is dangerous. Dialysis will help bring that down. We also gave you medicine to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already with the oxygen. But my chest still hurts sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG. You’re in atrial flutter with a fast heart rate. That could be causing the chest pain. Nitroglycerin didn’t help, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, didn’t do much. But the Dilaudid helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep using small doses for comfort. Your troponin is slightly elevated, but given your history, that’s often baseline for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. Your echo shows your heart function is stable, around 35-40%. The fluid overload and fast heart rate are the main issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your second X-ray shows the fluid is still there, maybe a bit worse on the right side. We’re starting antibiotics just in case there’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I don’t have a cough or sputum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did have yellow mucus yesterday. We sent a sputum test, but it didn’t show bacteria. Still, with your history, we don’t want to take chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. When’s dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later this morning. After that, you should start feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Breathing’s easier. Still a bit tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your labs show your potassium is down to 6.9 and creatinine improved. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate spiked to 160 last night. We gave you IV diltiazem and increased your daily dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s when the chest pain came back. Is the new dose safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we increased it to 420mg daily, taken at noon. We also adjusted when you take digoxin—now every other day and after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your digoxin level was high. Taking it after dialysis and every other day will keep it safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I still take my Percocet for the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched to oxycodone-acetaminophen. Take it as needed before and after dialysis. But the pain should improve as your heart rate stays under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to remove your tunneled dialysis catheter today. You have a working fistula, so you don’t need it anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local anesthesia. It’s a quick procedure. Some patients say chest pain improves after removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter’s out. You did great. The site looks clean, and your follow-up X-ray shows the lungs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel lighter. No chest pain since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows continued improvement in lung fluid. You’re breathing well on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You need one more dialysis and to stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Potassium is 4.9, creatinine 7.3. Your heart rate is staying in the 80s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more chest pain. I’ve been walking in the hall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll stop the antibiotics tomorrow since your blood cultures were negative and no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your diltiazem daily at noon, digoxin every other day after dialysis. Go to all your dialysis sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no cocaine. I know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s likely why your heart rate spikes and you end up here. Also, weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your breathing is normal, heart rate stable, and labs improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll stick to the plan this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Follow up with nephrology and your primary doctor. Stay away from cocaine—it’s harming your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge summary and prescriptions. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic systolic heart failure, and atrial fibrillation was admitted for shortness of breath and left-sided chest pain after missing a dialysis session due to diarrhea. He had used crack cocaine the morning before admission, which contributed to atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response. On arrival, he was hypoxic with bilateral pulmonary edema on chest X-ray and severe hyperkalemia. He was treated with oxygen, started on broad-spectrum antibiotics due to concern for pneumonia, and underwent hemodialysis, which improved his respiratory status and electrolyte abnormalities. His chest pain, reproducible on palpation and associated with tachycardia, improved after removal of his tunneled dialysis catheter and better rate control. His diltiazem dose was increased to 420mg daily taken at noon, and digoxin was adjusted to every other day post-dialysis due to a high trough level. Antibiotics were discontinued after negative blood cultures and clinical improvement. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to adhere to dialysis, avoid cocaine, monitor weight, and follow up with outpatient care.
